questions.q: Why does this lesson say a review-board presentation needs a different structure than the ADR document from Lesson 9?
options: Because a presentation is live and time-boxed, and a reviewer won't wait through several minutes of background before learning the actual decision, unlike a document read at the reader's own pace
Because ADRs are never shown to review boards
Because presentations should never mention failure modes
Because review boards only accept video recordings, never live presentations
questions.explain: A document can be read and re-read at the reader's own pace; a live presentation is time-boxed and interruptible, so structuring it like a document -- background first, decision last -- risks running out of time before the actual decision gets covered.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend opening a presentation with, and why?
options: A detailed history of every meeting that led to the decision
A full reading of the ADR's context section word for word
The one-sentence version of the decision itself, before the journey that produced it, so every later detail lands as support for something the reviewer already understands
An apology for any remaining unresolved issues
questions.explain: Leading with the decision means stating the conclusion first. Everything explained afterward then supports something the reviewer already has in mind, rather than building toward a reveal a live, time-boxed audience doesn't have patience for.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend naming a rejected alternative before being asked about it?
options: Because reviewers are forbidden from asking about alternatives
Because it signals the decision was actually tested against something and takes the single most predictable question off the table before it costs presentation time
Because alternatives should never actually be considered during design
Because naming an alternative guarantees the reviewer will approve the design
questions.explain: Experienced reviewers will ask about an obvious alternative if it isn't addressed. Naming it briefly and explaining why it lost, before being asked, signals real rigor and avoids losing time to a predictable question.

questions.q: If a presenter runs out of time partway through, what does this lesson say should survive the cut before detailed context does?
options: Nothing should ever be cut from a prepared presentation
Only the background and context sections should survive
The presenter should stop entirely and reschedule if any time runs short
The decision, the rejected alternative, and the failure-mode summary, because a reviewer can often infer enough context from the decision but can't infer the decision from the context
questions.explain: The lesson argues that the decision, the rejected alternative, and the failure-mode summary carry more value under time pressure than detailed background, since a reviewer can often work backward to enough context from the decision itself, but not forward from context to the decision.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say naming your own genuinely open question during a presentation is usually a good idea, not a weakness?
options: Because naming it yourself, before a reviewer finds it independently, reads as self-awareness rather than a claim of total, possibly false, confidence
Because reviewers always ignore stated open questions entirely
Because every presentation is required to include at least one unresolved issue
Because open questions make a presentation shorter
questions.explain: Surfacing a real open question yourself demonstrates the self-review from Lesson 10 actually happened. A presentation that claims total confidence about an area that's genuinely still thin is a bigger risk than one that's honest about where remaining uncertainty sits.
